items.title: Carl and Laura Lentz Speak Out About ‘Darkness,’ Hope Years After Scandal — and Offer a Path for ‘Overcoming Infidelity’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "It's almost like the most defeating, shame spiral you could ever imagine."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Carl Lentz was a preacher who seemed to have it all, until a moral failure forced him out as lead pastor of Hillsong NYC/East Coast.

His shocking firing rocked the evangelical world. Six years later, Lentz is sharing his healing journey. He and his wife, Laura, have a new book, “Overcoming Infidelity: 10 Conversations to Help You Heal the Hurt,” which helps guide people through the process.

Carl told CBN News they wrote the book to share their perspective and help others “make a dark season lighter.”

“We wanted to help people as fast as we could because we don’t think that you can get through it without help,” he said. “And we wanted to put as much as we’ve learned, and learn, and are currently learning, on paper.”

Carl said they hope to redeem what happened by helping others navigate similar struggles. Laura said she has received multitudes of messages from people over the past few years asking questions and seeking assistance.

Her experience has equipped her to guide others through the unthinkable, especially considering the very public nature of Carl’s affair — something that forced her to deal with other layers people in similar situations might not face.

“Finding out that you’ve been betrayed is really hard,” she said. “It’s awful. I wouldn’t wish it on anyone, but the public part was really hard, because you have extra voices coming at you, and giving their opinions, and their hate, and what they think, that’s confusing as well, and hurtful.”

Ultimately, Laura said it was a “very lonely road,” but one she was able to navigate. She said “it was very dark” before she found out what was truly happening in her husband’s life.

“A week before everything came out, I was in the shower just crying out to God. I was just like, God, whatever’s going on in him, just get it out,” she said. “You could see it in his eyes. His eyes had no life left. … I would look in his eyes and .. it was just darkness there.”

Once the truth came out, everything made more sense.

For Carl, the public piece of the puzzle was obviously quite intense. At first, despite the pain and sorrow, he said there was a relief that the truth had been revealed. That left him thinking, “Well, my life’s over, and I’m just gonna try to do what I can, patch this up, and I’m just gonna go off into a hole.” The journey from there wasn’t easy.

“It’s almost like the most defeating, shame spiral you could ever imagine,” Carl said. “In regard to the humiliation, I think I was not in a good place in my soul, so I didn’t care.”

He didn’t realize at the time, due to the state of his heart, mind, and soul, the impact the ordeal would have on his family.

“I wasn’t prepared for the impact on my family,” he said. “I just wasn’t. That’s the honest truth. … I didn’t care about what people were saying. It was more about the impact on my kids and my wife.”

Looking back, Carl said he truly believes he wasn’t well at the time of his moral failing. He said he faced an “avalanche of despair” in the wake of the chaos.

“I don’t even feel like I was in my right mind, and a part of me is grateful, because I feel like … if you’re living with that kind of duplicity and you can function, I don’t know what the future is for somebody like that,” he said. “There was help I could have gotten, there were people I could have talked to, there were better avenues.”

The natural question many have for the Lentzes: what led them to stay together after such a horrific public journey?

“I got some advice early on, which was really helpful for me, not to make any big decisions right away, any big life-altering decisions,” Laura said. “Just to take it a day at a time.”

Meanwhile, Carl went on a healing journey to address the past and present issues he was experiencing, including past childhood abuse. Laura said it was not an excuse for behavior but was helpful to understanding him.

“It … just kind of gave me a little bit more context as to how broken he was and …. hurt was inside of him that he’s never talked about,” she said, noting that she didn’t want to leave in those early moments and instead took the advice to take it day by day.

Carl also reflected on seeing help and healing his marriage.

“I got some immediate help and uncovered some things that, again, for anybody listening, when you explain context, it’s never an excuse,” he said. “It doesn’t matter what the context is. Unacceptable choices were made by me.”

Ultimately, Carl was able to ask some important questions about how he ended up in that position and why he made the choices he did. As for church accountability, Carl didn’t place blame on anyone other than himself.

“I had a great system around me,” he said. “Accountability is so worthless if people are not honest with themselves.”

The couple hopes that being open and candid and writing “Overcoming Infidelity: 10 Conversations to Help You Heal the Hurt” will help others facing similar circumstances.

“We’re just doing what God’s called us to do in this chapter,” Carl said. “We’ve written a book, and we want to tell people about it and get the word out, and if someone wants to talk, we’re gonna talk.”

items.title: Frank Turek Fights ‘War on Reality,’ Offers Warning for America
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "Dystopia"
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Apologist Frank Turek is on a mission to tackle the “war on reality,” warning Americans face a “dystopia” if the nation continues marching toward Marxism.

Turek’s new book, “The War on Reality Workbook: Recovering Truth in a World That Celebrates Lies,” is being released as the nation recently remembered the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative and Christian commentator Charlie Kirk.

The apologist told CBN News he and his coauthor, Phoenix Hayes, dedicated the book to Kirk, calling the late Turning Point USA founder a “warrior for reality.”

Turek broke down the current state of culture and decried many elements that simply make no logical — or biblical — sense.

“Abortion is healthcare; we’re pulling baby body parts out of women, and we’re calling that health care,” he said. “That’s a war on reality, and Charlie was a casualty in the war on reality. But, thankfully, since he was a believer, all the murderer was able to do is change his address.”

Turek continued, “He’s absent from the body, present with the Lord, and we remain behind, still engaged in fighting for reality when so many forces are fighting against.”

items.title: Bring Your Bible and Your Shotgun: Meet the Most Florida Church Plant Ever
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Sunday services at TruLife Church of Ocala’s newest campus come with a soundtrack of shotguns going off in the distance. Some attendees bring their own and check them at a rack by the door, the way other congregations check strollers. The campus is called BlackJack, like the range it meets at: Black
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Sunday services at TruLife Church of Ocala’s newest campus come with a soundtrack of shotguns going off in the distance. Some attendees bring their own and check them at a rack by the door, the way other congregations check strollers.

The campus is called BlackJack, like the range it meets at: Blackjack Sporting Clays, a shooting facility in Sumterville, Fla. The facility’s owners came up with the idea and asked pastor Michael Kirby about starting a church plant on the property. Kirby has a handy comparison for the place, which has four courses and a cart. “You rent a golf cart and you drive around and shoot clays at all the different posts,” he said. “It’s like playing golf, but you’re playing with a shotgun.” So it’s golf, but the clubs go off.

The sanctuary, loosely speaking, is a pavilion enclosed in thick, clear plastic, with mobile air conditioners keeping the cool air in and the wooded views visible. An 80-inch TV and a full sound system play Kirby’s prerecorded sermon three weeks a month, so three Sundays out of four the preacher arrives by screen. He or another TruLife pastor preaches live once a month, and Kirby’s daughter-in-law, Taylor Kirby, leads worship. Seating is about 40.

The church held a soft opening a couple of months ago and had its official launch on Sunday, Oct. 25, with Kirby preaching and a picnic lunch afterward. The day before, during a national competitive shooting event at the facility, volunteers handed out flyers and went door to door in the neighborhood, which is outreach with an unusually loud backdrop.

The target audience is the person who came to shoot. “We are hoping to attract unchurched people who are coming to BlackJack to do some shooting,” Kirby said. “Maybe they wouldn’t want to go to your typical church, but they decide they could go over here under the pavilion and hang out.” Evangelism by proximity, in other words: set up next to the people with the shotguns and hope they wander over.

Some of them already have noticed the music. Kirby says shooters have told him they can hear the worship from the service, and he is counting on it. “They might not come inside yet, but they’ll be out there worshipping in the middle of the grass,” he said. The worship set, it turns out, doubles as the range’s ambient soundtrack.

items.title: After Election Night, Remember, Christ the King Remains
items.author: Dr. Kody W. Cooper
items.summary:
Dr. Kody W. Cooper

An electorate that pretty handily returned Trump to power in 2024 has clearly rebuked him in 2026.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Kody W. Cooper

As I prepared for what promised and turned out to be foreboding election returns, I mixed up a couple of Rex Regum (King of Kings) cocktails for myself and a friend. And I recalled election night 2016 almost exactly a decade ago, for it was the last time I had this drink.

In the lead-up to the election of 2016, the traditional Christian outlook and way of life in America was, to use a boxing metaphor, “on the ropes.” The American Left had aggressively pushed cultural liberalism. From mandating the Little Sisters of the Poor pay for contraceptives, to kicking Catholic Charities out of adoption programs in states like Massachusetts and Illinois, to threatening the livelihood of Christian bakers and other proprietors if they did not genuflect and profess their faith in the creeds of cultural liberalism, it was no exaggeration to think that religious freedom in America was in the balance, since the winner would have a chance to shape the Supreme Court for a generation. Trump’s win was a shock to most observers (even to those of us who predicted he would win). It wasn’t clear that he would actually govern conservatively or nominate originalist judges to the courts who would restrain cultural liberalism. But there was at least a chance he would be, as the great Charles Krauthammer put it then, a junkyard bulldog who would protect traditional Christians from the predations of cultural liberalism.

As I sipped my Rex Regum, I couldn’t help but riff on Jacopo’s line to Edmund Dantes in The Count of Monte Cristo, when Dantes’s beloved Mercedes narrowly dodges a fatal bullet: “Once again, God sees America out of the corner of his eye. She will live.”

Ten years later, the landscape is very different. Cultural liberalism only metastasized during Trump I and bided its time until the Biden years, which saw virulent expression in the excesses of wokeness and identity politics. Still, Trump’s three Supreme Court picks, which will likely turn out to be his most important legacy, managed to overturn Roe, proved largely successful in keeping cultural liberalism in check at the legal level and expanded the capacity for those of traditional religious outlook to pursue happiness. And, since Trump’s comeback victory in 2024, the DOJ has arrested wokeism in many ways that have been broadly popular among Americans.

Rightly or wrongly, in such a landscape, the threat from the cultural Left is perceived to be diminished, weakened. More urgent to voters was the economy and cost of living—and Americans’ belief that Trump would deliver the material prosperity he promised in 2024. The exit polls reveal that the economy and cost of living drove the blue tsunami, more than any other single issue (including corruption, the Iran War, health care, immigration enforcement, etc.). According to exit polls, 66 percent of voters believe Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions and 63 percent blame Trump for higher prices, and a solid plurality (43 percent) said the Democratic Party would better handle the economy. It also looks like many voters believed Trump’s Iran War and tariffs have contributed to higher prices and economic woes. Exit polls found 74 percent of voters considered the Iran war to be a crucial or major factor in their vote; and 66 percent of voters believed the tariffs hurt the economy—Democrats won strong majorities of both of these groups.

The blue tsunami of 2026 is a historic reckoning. Democrats gained at least seven seats in the Senate (including “red” seats Trump won handily in Kansas, Ohio, Iowa, Texas, and South Carolina), at least twenty-one seats in the House, and flipped governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Texas, and Nevada. It was a “shellacking,” the most recent parallel of which was the red wave of 2014. Now, both parties are at a crossroads. 

The Republican Party in some states (like Texas) has been in power so long that it has too often lost its immunity to internal rot. A candidate like Ken Paxton—a flagrant adulterer and uninspiring goober who was credibly accused of corruption—was an electoral turd that hundreds of millions of dollars could not polish. In South Carolina, Darlene Graham basically admitted she was unqualified to succeed her brother. Both were endorsed by Trump. Even if alternative choices in these races would not have survived the blue tsunami, clearly the GOP has a candidate quality problem that goes to the top. An electorate that pretty handily returned Trump to power in 2024 has clearly rebuked him in 2026. This comes two years after they gave Republicans united government, whose biggest legislative accomplishment, the so-called Big Beautiful Bill, was referred to as a crap sandwich even by its defenders. So, what kind of party will the GOP be in the post-Trump era? Can it recover a coherent conservatism which prizes constitutionalism, limited government, personal and public virtue, ordered liberty, and the hardscrabble but unsexy work of member wrangling, negotiation, compromise, and competently legislating? Or will it succumb to opportunistic disrespect for rule of law, licentiousness, superficial kayfabe, grift, and incompetence? 

The Democratic Party is also at a crossroads. How will it exert its newfound power? For it elected candidates who are at least as ostensibly different as Abdul El Sayed, James Talarico, and Josh Turek. El Sayed is a democratic socialist-adjacent candidate who in the final days of the campaign expressed his communistic view that children belong to the collective and parents don’t have the right to shield their children from the detritus of cultural liberalism in public schools because they don’t even have such a duty. El Sayed went so far as to say that the parental duty to protect their children’s innocence was an “outdated” idea. Talarico is a pro-abortion radical who has argued that God is pro-choice, since he gave the Blessed Virgin Mary a choice whether to bear the Son of God and suggested that being created in God’s image means that human beings are essentially genderless. Meanwhile, Josh Turek, the Paralympian—who explicitly eschewed being a “liberal” and campaigned as a moderate “Prairie Populist”—largely avoided speaking about or voting on the controversial culture and war issues. Will the Democratic Party learn from the backlash to Woke 1.0; rediscover the honorable strains of progressive and centrist liberalism of statesmen like FDR, Kennedy, Moynihan, and Clinton; and focus on the thoughtful reforms advanced by liberal public intellectuals like Matt Yglesis and Ezra Klein? Will they focus on popular economic policies and restrain the drive of its most radical members towards aggressive cultural liberalism? Or will the Party embrace Woke 2.0, a more radical version of the original?
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

While we cannot know the answers to these questions, we can take solace in knowing who is really in charge and recalling what this means for the Christian. In Quas Primas, wherein the Church established the Feast of Christ the King, Pope Pius XI taught that Christ’s kingship is over all things, including our politics. In his person is embodied supreme legislative, executive, and judicial power. It is a spiritual kingdom, which demands of its subjects “a spirit of detachment from riches and earthly things, and a spirit of gentleness,” who, at the same time, “must hunger and thirst after justice, and more than this, they must deny themselves and carry the cross.” So Christians must work for justice—must seek to align human law and policy with the eternal law—and be willing to sacrifice for justice and the common good of their polity. This vocation is quickened by and ordered to Christ’s kingship. For if a person in whose heart Jesus reigns is an instrument of peace, will not a society of men and women in whose hearts Christ reigns have the tranquility of peace? And yet Christians can only ever have one foot in this world, for their ultimate hope lies in the desire of another. 

As we celebrate the Feast of Christ the King this November, let us never forget: The fortunes of earthly politics wax and wane, but the virtue of hope in Christ the King remains.

items.title: ‘Nor Can Foot Feel, Being Shod’: The Theology of Feet
items.author: Dr. Chad Engelland
items.summary:
Dr. Chad Engelland

It is instructive that the very evening in which our Lord set apart his priests and their hands for the breaking of the bread, he also washes their feet.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Chad Engelland

In what follows, I want to add a footnote to Pope St. John Paul II’s meditation on the spiritual significance of our bodies, which makes manifest our vocation to love. Though seemingly unimportant, the foot is indeed something to note. 

This point was lost on me for most of my life, but two years ago, I found myself unable to think about anything other than feet and their theology. Collapsed on the grass at the end of an exhausting two-day, thirty-five-mile pilgrimage here in the US, my own feet aching and blistered, I beheld a scene that transported me to Sant’Agostino in Rome, which not only boasts the mortal remains of St. Monica but also a stunning image by Caravaggio.

There before me I saw in the flesh the very feet of Caravaggio’s pilgrim in his painting Madonna of the Pilgrims, also known as Madonna of Loretto. Not only were the feet in front of me bare and dirty, the bottoms faced me as the pilgrim in question knelt in reverence at Mass.

Behold feet! The baby, the toddler, and the young child have adorable feet. Yet when these same feet achieve adult form, they almost invariably lose their beauty and take on a purely functional character, just like elbows and ears.

Caravaggio’s masterful painting brilliantly highlights this very contrast between young and old, for he places in the Madonna’s hands the infant Christ, whose cherubic feet dangle effortlessly in the arms of his mother; her own pristine feet, in turn, are elevated above the earth, both by a step and by their position—as though she were calmly supported only by her toes. Yet the pilgrim’s feet are dirty, flexed, and strained, pressed down by the burden of being.

Though the feeling of feet would have been a daily occurrence for much of human history, we moderns have had to pay little attention to our feet. As the poet Gerard Manley Hopkins notes in “God’s Grandeur,” they are insulated from our notice: “Nor can foot feel, being shod.” Shoes anesthetize our feet, keeping them snug, safe, and squarely outside of our notice.

I Am My Feet

The great French Catholic philosopher Gabriel Marcel might have said, “I am my body,” but we pilgrims could put that same line more pointedly as “I am my feet.” When we do so, what might we note?

First, feet are for standing. One of the glories of parenting is having one’s child stand in that first wobbly, swaying posture, an act repeated every morning by each of us as long as we are able. To stand again each day is a natural rehearsal for the resurrection on the last day.

Second, feet are for walking. Another of the glories of parenting is having one’s child take his or her first steps, something each of us repeats again and again throughout our days. To walk here and there is the natural analogue to our daily spiritual journey to our heavenly homeland.

Third, feet are for feeling. Stand too much and the feet hurt. Walk too far and the feet hurt. Run too hard and the feet hurt. At such moments, we may even be tempted to wonder: Do we have hands just to massage our aching feet? To suffer through one’s feet is to be constantly reminded that we need to lift our hearts to the Lord.

Fourth, feet are for virtue. If humility is the key to all virtues, feet are supremely important. It’s true our physiological demands are humbling as well, but the plain fact that we have feet—feet that press down again and again into the humus of the earth—is a reminder that whatever our ultimate heavenly aspiration, we are also terrestrial creatures and not angels. 

Fifth, feet are for reverence. Whether we sit or stand, our feet are on the ground, ready to take us off walking at a moment’s notice. But when we kneel, we introduce a further remove: Our feet are out of commission. To walk, we first have to stand up, one leg at a time. Kneeling, then, is from one point of view the feet offering themselves up by shifting weight from their soles to the knees. To kneel is to plant oneself in the earth and be still.

Sixth, feet are for the whole person. Each of us pilgrims are one body with many parts. There may be some parts more noble than others, but their very nobility depends for their exercise on the whole and its lowliest parts. “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you,’ nor again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need of you.’” (1 Cor 12:21). That is, we can only hold our head high if our feet are keeping us humbly planted below.

And They Kissed His Feet and Worshipped Him

Jesus’s feet bore the weight of the cross, and thus for good reason did Mary anoint them with precious oil (John 11:2). And when he is restored to life, he shows not only his hands but also his feet to his disciples. “Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

On the Friday that we call Good, we each take turns kissing the feet of the corpus on the crucifix.

It is instructive that the very evening in which our Lord set apart his priests and their hands for the breaking of the bread, he also washes their feet. They were in Jerusalem on pilgrimage. Theirs were the feet of figures on the way, and those feet would soon take those hands to the four corners of the earth.

Perhaps we might recall, in this connection, the wisdom that St. Paul drew from Isaiah: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!” (Rom 10:15, quoting Isa 52:7). 

A Note About Hobbits

Allow me to close this footnote about feet with an asterisk about hobbits, for J. R. R. Tolkien seems to have divined the spiritual significance of feet when he brought this species into being. Hobbits have as their most distinctive bodily feature, besides their diminutive size, large bare feet. And it was those very feet that, step by step, enacted the first adventure of Bilbo from the Shire to the Lonely Mountain and back again, and those very sort of feet that made the all-important pilgrimage that destroyed the ring. The hobbits, we can say, represent the human as pilgrim, setting out to destroy, through humility, the allure and weight of sin. Their pilgrimage, like every other, was a kind of via crucis.
